subject: forestSpirit
pitch: A small forest spirit, part deer and part mossy stone. A body of grey river stone covered in soft green moss, slender wooden legs ending in little hooves, branching antlers sprouting tiny white flowers and leaves, a pale wooden mask-like face with two glowing green eyes, and a few fireflies circling its head.
reasoning:
I'm designing a forest spirit creature—a deer-stone hybrid about 1.4 m tall including antlers, standing on the ground plane, using the 3js builder SDK to construct it.

Orientation is +Z facing with +X as left, so I need named joints organized into chains with clear roles for a rest pose of extended legs and separated head/jaw parts. The mouth needs separate upper and lower jaw joints so it can open, even with a pale wooden mask-style face.

For the fireflies circling the head, I'm thinking of small glowing spheres placed on a ring of frames around the head joint, since the builder requires all geometry to attach through joints rather than existing as free-floating props.

For glowing eyes, since the SDK doesn't directly expose emissive material properties through the color string API, I could create the eye part normally and then manually override its mesh's material afterward with a custom emissive MeshStandardMaterial to get that glow effect.

For the body, I'm planning to build it as a lumpy river stone shape using mottled grey paint for texture, then layer mossy green patches on upward-facing surfaces using normal-based blending so moss naturally appears on top like it would on a real stone.

I'm also double-checking the SDK's exports to make sure the color-mixing `mix` function from paint takes precedence over the bone-weight `mix` from context, so I avoid accidentally using the wrong one.

Instead of hard-switching between moss and stone paints based on a coverage threshold, I'm blending them smoothly by sampling both paints at a point and interpolating their resulting colors with `mix`, which keeps the transition natural rather than creating a sharp edge.

Now I'm shifting focus to actually designing the character itself — thinking through its proportions in meters, aiming for a deer-like body about 0.9m long with shoulders around 0.55m high, and sketching out the skeleton hierarchy starting from a pelvis root joint and building a spine chain forward toward the chest and neck using a curved path of joints.

I'm working out how to structure the leg chains so each has a hip, knee, ankle, and hoof-tip joint properly placed along the limb's path.

For the legs themselves I'm planning slender wooden limbs with tapering radius from top to ankle, wood grain texture, and small dark hooves at the tips. For the body I'm considering a dodecahedron-based geometry to give it a stylized, faceted stone appearance.

I'm thinking of building the chest and hips from scaled dodecahedron shapes, plus adding mossy paint that reads automatically on upward-facing normals so moss appears naturally on top surfaces without needing separate geometry.

For the head, I'm considering a deer-skull-like elongated shape made from a scaled sphere, with a pale wooden mask face extruded as a flat plate on the front, possibly with eye hole cutouts in the outline.

I need to work out the right local axes so the mask extrudes facing forward along +Z rather than sideways, then sketch the face outline coordinates—wide at the forehead, narrowing toward the chin, sized roughly 0.2m by 0.26m, with glowing green sphere eyes set into dark recessed sockets and painted wood-grain lines on the mask surface.

I'm confirming the paint function gets surface coordinates for extruded geometry, so the mask can darken the eye socket regions while glowing green eye spheres sit in front. Now I'm sketching the overall body proportions — ground at hoof level, hip height, head and mask position — to lock in the full figure's composition before refining details.

Working through the leg joint coordinates: hip, knee, ankle, and hoof tip positions for front and hind legs, accounting for the hock bend on the hind legs and slight splay at the feet so the stance looks natural and grounded.

I'm now settling on naming conventions for the leg chain joints that a rigger would recognize—shoulder/knee/ankle/hoof for the front legs and hip/knee/hock/hoof for the hind legs.

Now I'm thinking through how to sweep tapered tube geometry along each leg chain so it bends smoothly at the joints, then figuring out how to attach small cylindrical hoof caps rigidly at the leg tips.

For the head and neck, I'm planning a short multi-segment chain running from the chest up through the neck to a head joint, deciding where each knot should sit so the proportions look natural and the head can aim forward correctly.

Now I'm working out how the skull and jaw attach: a jaw joint hanging off the head for mouth movement, and figuring out how the head's bone orientation should be set so the pale wooden mask-like face parts align properly on the front of the skull.

Since geometry I build in model space without an explicit quat stays in model orientation, I can rely on default identity rotation and just position parts correctly with `at`, letting them inherit bone transforms during posing. I'm planning to extrude the mask shape onto the head bone, then move on to building branching antler geometry sweeping up from the top of the skull.

Writing sweep-based antler code...

For the small decorative details, I'm thinking tiny white flower clusters made of small spheres, leaf shapes using thin planar slabs with custom outline points, and giving the antlers a darker wood tone with grain texture to contrast the pale mask. I need to stay mindful of the triangle and part budget, keeping things to roughly 150-200 parts, and I'm considering whether the deer needs a small tail or if I should skip it to save on complexity.

For fireflies I'm picturing five tiny glowing yellow-green spheres arranged in a ring around the head using a ring helper that positions items relative to a frame's axis, with the head joint's orientation determining whether the ring sits horizontal or tilted.

Actually, I think it's simpler to skip the ring helper entirely and just compute firefly positions manually in a loop—spreading them around a circle with some jitter for randomness, attached loosely to the head bone since they're decorative and don't need precise posing.

For the glow effect, I'll give the firefly material emissive properties so they look like they're lit up, swapping in a standard material with emissive color and intensity set directly on the mesh.

Now for the body, I'm constructing the stone chest from a low-poly dodecahedron shape, scaling it non-uniformly for a flattened, stylized look, and making sure normals compute correctly since the geometry isn't indexed.

Since dodecahedron faces aren't axis-aligned, the chart projection will foreshorten oblique faces and give uneven texel density, but that's acceptable for this look. I could instead make moss as separate green primitives layered on the grey stone rather than painting, which is simpler and fits a blocky style, but painted moss blending onto the stone looks nicer, so I'll go with the paint approach.

For resolution, I'm weighing 1024 vs 2048 paint sheets—2048 gives better detail but with noise and cellular hashing per texel across 4M pixels, bake time could balloon, so I'll default to 1024 for safety and add separate small green icosahedron moss tufts on top for extra detail.

For the legs and antlers, I'll give them grain-painted wood rather than solid color, though their surface area is small enough that it shouldn't add much to the overall texture sheet.

Now I'm laying out the body's stone components concretely: a chest dodecahedron stone forward, a rump stone behind, and a belly stone connecting them, each positioned and scaled along the Z-axis to form an elongated stylized torso.

I'm adding small mossy pebble stones along the back ridge, then working out how the legs join the body -- placing front leg joints (shoulder, knee, ankle, hoof) and hind leg joints (hip, stifle, hock, hoof) at specific x/y/z coordinates so they tuck inside the body's width and align with the chest and rump stone positions, checking that the belly height and leg-top placement look anatomically plausible for a stylized stone deer.

Now I'm planning how to generate the mirrored leg chains programmatically, using a side parameter to flip x-coordinates for left/right legs, naming each joint according to the allowed naming pattern, and sweeping a tapered radius profile (thicker at the hip, narrower toward the hoof) along each leg's path.

I'm figuring out how the sweep's round caps interact with the hoof geometry at the leg's tip — making sure the hoof cylinder covers the rounded bottom cap so the leg blends cleanly into the hoof, then sizing the hoof as a small tapered cylinder positioned at the ground. I'm also starting to plan the head's position, setting joint coordinates for the neck and head so they connect naturally before adding antlers, flowers, and leaves.

The jaw's hinge axis is set along the horizontal left-right direction. For the overall head design, I'm thinking the mask could be a separate pale-wood plate layered onto the front of a mossy-stone skull, with the lower jaw as a smaller wood piece beneath it, and the muzzle protruding forward as its own rounded shape in front of the skull sphere.

Working out exact placement so the mask plate sits proud of the muzzle without being swallowed by it, adjusting the skull, muzzle, and mask z-coordinates until they layer correctly front-to-back.

Actually, since this is a stylized blocky puppet, a box-shaped head fits better than curved shapes — I'll try a cranium box with the mask as a flat plate on its front face and a narrower muzzle box projecting forward, though I need to work out how they meet without awkward overlap.

Mapping the geometry: mask plate sits just in front of the cranium's face, sized to cover forehead-to-chin, while a tapered frustum box forms the snout emerging from behind it toward the nose tip. The snout pokes slightly through the mask plate, which I think can read as the nose breaking through the mask rather than clipping error.

For color, I'm painting both the mask plate and the snout the same pale wood tone so they visually read as one continuous piece rather than separate parts. Eyes will be small glowing green spheres set into the mask near the top of the outline, with dark painted sockets around them for contrast.

For the wood grain and markings, I'm setting the mask's base coloring and planning out the eye socket positions within the outline's coordinate frame, making sure the paint function's local coordinates line up correctly with where the extrude places the eyes in model space.

Now I'm working out how to build the deer ears using leaf-shaped slabs projecting out from the skull — defining base and tip points for each ear so the slab geometry closes properly without needing explicit normal orientation.

For the antlers, I'm sketching branching paths from the base of the skull outward and upward, giving each beam curvature and adding secondary tines at points along the main beam, plus small white flower clusters and leaf details at the tips to match the mossy, overgrown look.

Thinking through flower construction...

I'll add green leaf slabs along the antler tines, shaping each as a small oriented polygon flaring out from an attach point with a defined width and length. For fireflies, I'm planning 5-6 tiny emissive yellow-green spheres circling near the head, positioned using a seeded random function for natural variation.

Now I'm working through the eyes, giving them a glowing green emissive color, then adding mossy texture details: flattened icosahedron clumps scattered on top of the stones for a 3D tufted look, keeping the base stone grey while the moss adds color on top. For the tail, I'm sketching a small moss-covered sweep shape built from a short polyline path tapering from the rump outward, using a swept capsule-like form with a mossy color and tapering radius.

I'm defining the paint systems next: a mottled grey stone paint and a mottled moss paint, then combining them into a composite "mossyStone" paint that blends grey and moss based on surface normal (favoring moss on upward-facing areas) plus some patchy noise-driven moss on the sides for a natural, weathered look. I'm also setting up a wood grain paint for the mask/snout/legs/antlers, and writing a custom paint function for the face mask that darkens into eye sockets with a smooth blend around the eye positions, using mix and smoothstep to fade between the dark socket color and the wood grain base.

Now I'm laying out the skeleton: a root pelvis joint, a spine chain running through the torso up to a "chest" tip joint, a neck chain continuing from the chest toward a head joint, with a jaw joint hinging below the head so the mouth can open as a separate upper and lower jaw. I'm thinking through how chain point counts and name arrays map to joint positions and tips, making sure positions aren't awkwardly duplicated between adjacent chains, and planning a mossy-stone sweep along the neck for visual continuity with the stone body.

I'm now defining the four-legged rig: front legs as shoulder-knee-ankle-hoof chains parented to the chest/spine, and hind legs as hip-stifle-hock-hoof chains parented to the pelvis, each with distinct left/right names and deer-like joint offsets for a believable stride stance. I'm placing small dark cylinder hooves at each leg's tip, and defining a tail chain off the pelvis with a tapering mossy sweep for a tuft-like tail.

I'm placing the mossy stone body masses -- rump, chest, belly, shoulder and hip bumps, and a few back-ridge accents -- as scaled dodecahedra positioned to approximate a deer-like silhouette, then defining a blocky box-shaped cranium for the head with a flat front face to host the wood-grain face mask plate, working out the mask's offset and size relative to the head box so it sits just in front of the skull without clipping awkwardly.

I'm designing the face mask as a 14-point rounded outline with light smoothing and a small bevel, sized to roughly match the head box's width with a bit of brow overhang, and placing glowing eye spheres in dark socket regions on the mask so they poke slightly out of the plate's front face.

I'm shaping a tapered muzzle as a frustum box extending forward from the head toward the mouth, choosing flat caps and binding it to the head bone, then adding a smaller lower jaw box bound to the jaw bone and a small dark nose sphere at the snout tip for detail. I'm sketching leaf-shaped ear slabs projecting from the sides of the head using a base-to-tip direction with a perpendicular offset to form a simple diamond leaf silhouette, colored mossy green and bound to the head bone.

I'm laying out the antlers as tapering swept beams rising from the top of the skull, branching into a few shorter tines, and reconsidering the overall height since the original antler reach made the creature taller than intended for a "small forest spirit" -- so I'm compressing the beam and tine coordinates to bring the total height down to a more modest scale while keeping the branching silhouette. I'm planning to scatter small five-petal flowers at the antler tips and a couple of mid-beam points, each built from a cluster of tiny petal spheres around a yellow center sphere, and adding a handful of leaf slabs along the tines using a similar base/dir/side point construction as the ears.

Finally, I'm working out firefly placement as small glowing spheres distributed in a rough ring around the head and antlers using randomized angle, radius, and height offsets so they hover near but not inside the skull geometry, with glow materials applied after creating each sphere part.

I'm also considering adding faint light-trail arcs behind each firefly to suggest motion, built as thin swept tubes along short orbital arc paths with their own glowing material swapped in after the sweep, though I'm weighing whether this adds too much complexity for the payoff. I'm placing mossy clumps as flattened icosahedra scattered across the stone body's shoulders, chest, and back ridge for texture variation between two green tones, and considering adding small moss-ring toruses around the leg joints, rotated so their axis wraps around the leg rather than lying flat, sized to just exceed the leg's local radius at that point.

I'm settling on paint definitions for the body: grainy wood textures for the legs and antlers with tuned grain sizes, a pale grain pattern for the mask/snout, solid dark color for the hooves and nose, and the mossy stone paint for the torso -- then thinking through how the baking system will chart and pack all these materials into a single texture sheet, estimating chart density and texel resolution to make sure the stone and wood grain details stay sharp enough at the given sheet size.

I'm also planning the module's export structure -- a meta object with name and description, and a default creature-building function that sets up the builder with appropriate detail and paint-sheet size before returning the baked root group -- and running through the necessary imports from three.js and the SDK.

I'm carefully cross-checking the builder API signatures for joints, chains, parts, sweeps, frustum boxes, extrusions, and slabs against how I'm using them, confirming that sweep radius arrays are valid inputs and that naming sweeps/parts will help with debugging.

I'm reasoning through how placing stones via nearest-joint weighting works when no explicit bone is given, and deciding to instead specify explicit bones for the chest and rump stones to keep the rig semantically clean, while double-checking that non-uniform scaling on the dodecahedron stones correctly transforms normals through the chartify/bake pipeline without introducing incorrect double-transformation of geometry when placing baked meshes under their bone's world transform.

I confirm that mesh geometry stays in local bone space while the separate "world" position array is only used for paint baking, and that extrude/slab functions correctly pass through surface UV data for paint lookups even when geometry gets converted to non-indexed form.

I define the paint functions: a mottled grey/moss combination for the stone body that favors moss on upward-facing and randomly patched areas, grainy wood colors for legs and antlers, a pale grain for the mask with darkened eye-socket rings computed from surface UV distance to each eye position, plus solid colors for leaves, flower centers, hooves, and moss clumps, and a small helper for making glowing emissive materials for the eyes and fireflies.

I start writing the actual builder code: setting up the pelvis root joint, then the spine chain, neck chain, head and jaw joints, and iterating over left/right sides to build mirrored front and hind leg chains with appropriately named joints for shoulder, knee, ankle, hip, stifle, and hock.

Writing leg chains and hoof geometry...
